newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary c.bank says growth will not hit forint.
newsitem.headline: Hungary c.bank says growth will not hit forint.

text.p: A senior Hungarian central bank official said on Wednesday the country's accelerating economic growth would not result in the same currency and current account problems dogging other countries in the region.
"We have not seen any speculation against the forint and also I do not see a chance for that in the future," National Bank of Hungary (NBH) Vice President Gyorgy Szapary told Reuters in an interview.
"The fundamentals of the economy are so favourable that these will not create a speculation wave similar to what happened in the Czech Republic and Poland."
Hungary projects gross domestic product (GDP) growth of three percent this year and four to five percent in the subsequent years, a sharp rise on the preliminary figure of one percent in 1996.
Similar growth explosions in Czech Republic and Poland have led to a marked rise in imports, sparking fears of trade and current account difficulties and weakening the crown and the zloty.
But Szapary said Hungary's dynamic export growth and maintained international competitiveness safeguarded the country against similar problems.

"I don't think that Hungary will face current account problems because of a pick-up in growth if exports continue to grow so quickly and I don't see a reason why they should not," he said, adding "There is no sign of a recession in Europe".
Hungary's current account deficit target for this year is $2 billion, slightly up from a $1.7 billion gap in 1996.

Szapary said a further reduction in Hungary's monthly crawling peg devaluation rate would depend on the rate of inflation. The monthly devaluation rate is due to be cut to one percent in August from the current 1.1 percent.

"The forint's depreciation must be in line with inflation and the increase in productivity in the economy," Szapary said, adding that Hungary's productivity growth has been the quickest in the region over the past few years.
"Currently the devaluation rate is lower than inflation but taking into account unit labour cost developments, the real exchange rate maintained international competitiveness," he added.

Szapary said that Hungary's forint had been pinned to the upper resistance level of the 4.5 percent wide floating intervention range over the past two years, only occasionally drifting away from the NBH bid.
"This shows clearly that the markets believe the forint will remain strong," Szapary said.
He said a widening of the 4.5 percent wide intervention band could give monetary policies greater room for manoeuvre.
"But there is no pressure for a widening," Szapary said.
